summary: South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 28, prepared by the National Economic Board, covers January 1948 for USAMGIK and the South Korean Interim Government, with some economic data for December 1947. The month was dominated by the arrival of the UN Temporary Commission on Korea, which shaped politics, the press and the Legislative Assembly. Economic reporting shows rice collection at 96.9 per cent of quota, falling coal, power and industrial output, rising prices (Seoul retail index 2,231) and a 60-fold electric rate increase, while note issue fell 1.77 billion won from its peak. Executive Order No. 12 reorganized consumer-goods allocation. Refugee inflow from the north dropped 45 per cent. A new section covers Women's Activities. Historians will find detailed price, trade, finance, labor, legislative and press-opinion material, including strikes, a rightist merger, North Korean radio propaganda, and public opinion polls on forced contributions.
highlights: The 1947/48 rice collection reached 749,313 metric tons, 96.9 per cent of the 773,477-ton quota, with Cholla-pukto lowest at 80.2 per cent; four months of undelivered rations were issued in January.

Executive Order No. 12 (12 January, signed by Maj. Gen. William F. Dean) created the Korean Government Employees Welfare Office and the seven-member Consumer Goods Allocation Board, abolishing the Civil Service Relief Committee.

Refugees entering South Korea from the north numbered 2,541 in January, down 45 per cent from December; the cumulative count since 1945 stood at 803,434, with 1,264,530 Koreans repatriated from abroad.

The Seoul retail price index (August 1945 = 100) reached 2,231 in January 1948 against 1,916 in December; on 8 January the Permanent Public Utilities Board recommended a roughly 60-fold rise in retail electric rates.
Anthracite output fell to 31,333 tons in December (12.2 per cent below November), 26.2 per cent short of quota, and bituminous imports from Japan reached only 44,452 tons against an expected 60,000.

Bank of Chosun notes outstanding fell 1,767,000,000 won in January from the December peak as the rice collection passed its high point; supplementary appropriations of over 601,000,000 won were approved.

Labor unrest included a Yong Dong Po strike at 12 factories (Kyungsung Textile, about 10,000 workers) and a Seoul streetcar walkout of 259 employees; the Tai Han No Chung Federation, 864 delegates, re-elected Chun Jin-han.

The UN Temporary Commission dominated politics: the Legislative Assembly often lacked a quorum, Kim Koo and Rhee Syngman merged rightist groups on 9 January, and Kim Koo urged troop withdrawal and a North-South leaders' conference.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Google Books pages, cover of No. 28 (January 1948) prepared by the National Economic Board, map legend, and contents for Parts I-VI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Editors' overview of winter 1947-48: falling industrial output and coal, the Bank of Chosun note-issue peak, social progress, new graphic tables and the new Women's Activities section.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population movement, Koreans abroad, 10,420 foreign residents, and vested property work, including Koreanization of companies and 30,263,000 won in January sales.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Southbound refugees fell to 2,541; 508,190 Koreans in Japan, with ten League of Korea members deported after the 20 December Tokyo riot; 419 Koreans travelled abroad; 10,420 foreigners resident.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody sold 39 properties for 30,263,000 won, audited 374 companies, pursued ghost companies, and held former Government General property for the successor Korean government.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: More than 20 per cent of vested industrial properties operating; almost half of ghost companies deactivated or rehabilitated; 30,000,000 won of enterprises passed to Korean management.

sections.title: Operations
sections.summary: Re-organization unit completed 129 preliminary investigations; six loan applications totalled 212,000,000 won, led by Korean Forwarding Co.; 1,381 financial statements received; over 40 ghost companies investigated.

sections.title: Property Disposal
sections.summary: Thirty-nine sales yielded 30,263,000 won, including five ships (7,993,000 won) and 11 residences; residence sales were delayed by appraisal difficulties.

sections.title: Audits and Inventories
sections.summary: Audits of 374 companies were in progress at 31 January; reports on 10 major companies were completed.

sections.title: Real Estate Requisitions
sections.summary: Twenty-six requisitions received and 15 releases effected for formerly Japanese property used by Occupation Forces; leases negotiated for adjoining Korean tracts.

sections.title: Provincial Affairs
sections.summary: Sixty-six field inspection trips checked inventory progress toward the 30 June 1948 deadline; transport was the main bottleneck and 400 bicycles were bought.

sections.title: Policies and Decisions
sections.summary: General Counsel policy: property registered to the Government General of Korea on 9 August 1945 will not be sold without approval of the owning government agency.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Food, prices, agriculture, mining, industry, allocations, trade and labor: rice collection 96.9 per cent, Seoul price index 2,231, coal shortfalls, Executive Order No. 12, 1947 trade totals, strikes.

sections.title: Section 1. Food Supply
sections.summary: Rice collection reached 749,313 tons (96.9 per cent of quota); stocks 636,757 tons; 76,586 tons rationed; first sugar (16,127 tons) and dried milk imports arrived.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: At 31 January the rice quota was 96.9 per cent complete; sugar and dried milk were on hand; the ration population probably rose.

sections.title: January Transactions
sections.summary: January collections of 81,832 tons of polished rice, distribution of 76,586 tons, and month-end stocks of 636,757 tons.

sections.title: Trends
sections.summary: Rice distribution rose steadily over six months, other grains nearly ran out, and ration population stayed frozen at 9,476,856 since October; 510,524 suk released in January.

sections.title: Rice Collections
sections.summary: Most provinces exceeded quota; Cholla-pukto reached only 80.2 per cent while Chungchong-pukto reached 117.9 per cent.

sections.title: Imports
sections.summary: January grain imports of 37,849 tons: wheat 17,269, rice 3,076, dry milk 2,907 and sugar 16,127 tons.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Seoul retail index rose to 2,231 in January (1,916 in December) on scarcity, hoarding and fear of currency flows from the north; wholesale prices rose faster; National Price Administration fixed prices.

sections.title: Retail Prices
sections.summary: Among 26 Seoul items only rubber shoes and firewood fell; soy beans, sesame oil, leather shoes and silk rose sharply; index tables run January 1946 to January 1948.

sections.title: Wholesale Prices
sections.summary: Seoul wholesale index for 27 items rose faster than retail from October to January, led by barley, soy beans, cotton yarn, lumber, cement and copper.

sections.title: Controlled Prices
sections.summary: Controlled retail prices for rice and some rationed goods damped open-market increases; wholesale index tables for 27 commodities follow.

sections.title: Activities, National Price Administration
sections.summary: Price-setting examples: wool serge at 200 won per yard, Puksan paper at 66 won per pound; tables of controlled prices to 31 January 1948.

sections.title: Section 3. Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: 1948 production goals, 63,710 tons of ammonium sulphate agreed, Ordinance No. 165 reorganizing the Korean Agricultural Association, and a New Korea Company census of 619,000 farms.

sections.title: Agricultural Economics
sections.summary: Crop reporting reorganized under Ordinance 143; summer-grain acreage fell short of 1948 goals; a grain inspector school trained 1,417 inspectors.

sections.title: Agricultural Production
sections.summary: 1,245 dairy cattle, pyrethrum on Cheju-do, 5,628,000 keun of seed cotton collected, silk exported to Hong Kong for rubber, and irrigation contracts.

sections.title: Forestry
sections.summary: Fuelwood goals for winter 1947/48 were reached, though transport limited city supplies; forest production figures given for October and November 1947.

sections.title: Fisheries
sections.summary: 272,760 bundles of laver shipped to Japan; marine product goals set to 1953; 13,000,000 won fisheries training budget approved.

sections.title: Korea Agricultural Association
sections.summary: SCAP agreed to ship 63,710 tons of ammonium sulphate; 241,181 tons of fertilizer moved to railheads; seed potato losses ran 6-10 per cent.

sections.title: New Korea Company
sections.summary: Ordinance 165 revised the Association's chain of authority; first post-liberation census counted 619,000 NKC farms averaging 0.87 chungbo per tenant.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite 31,333 tons in December, 26.2 per cent below quota; Samchuk Mine failed; bituminous imports 44,452 tons; pitch shortage halted briquettes; tungsten and copper problems.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: December data came from large repossessed mines and a few private units. South Korean coal is all poor anthracite and lignite, so imported bituminous coal matters more than local output.

sections.title: Indigenous Anthracite and Lignite Coal
sections.summary: Anthracite fell 12.2 per cent on power cuts and truck shortages; Samchuk made 13,392 tons against a 25,000-ton quota; stockpiles of 160,000 tons.

sections.title: Bituminous Coal
sections.summary: Japanese imports of 44,452 tons were 31.4 per cent below December; 6,000 tons allocated to industry; tables of shipments since October 1945.

sections.title: Pitch
sections.summary: Imported pitch ran out, cutting briquette output; the National Coal Committee allocated pitch like coal, and briquette factories moved under Commerce's Chemical Section.

sections.title: Other Minerals
sections.summary: Kimbuk copper suffered car shortages, three copper mines might close, and the Dalsung tungsten mine (40,000,000 won rehabilitation) sat idle for lack of power.

sections.title: Section 5. Industrial Production
sections.summary: December output fell on cold, coal and power shortages: flour 51 per cent of November, cotton yarn down 28.4 per cent, paper 171.8 tons, briquettes down 42.5 per cent; cement rose to 3,251 tons.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Data cover perhaps 10 per cent of plants; cold, snow and electricity shortage caused drastic production declines.

sections.title: Processed Food
sections.summary: Flour fell to 51 per cent of November for lack of wheat; six small mills produced only 210 tons; noodle output down 27.3 per cent.

sections.title: Textiles
sections.summary: Ten plants reported cotton yarn, output 28.4 per cent below November; mixed cotton and flax cloth totalled 17,506 meters.

sections.title: Paper
sections.summary: Machine-made paper reached 171.8 tons in December, lowest since February 1947, owing to pulp and power scarcity.

sections.title: Hardware
sections.summary: Nail production fell 14.7 per cent to 161.2 tons, with all three plants limited by coal and power.

sections.title: Chemical Group
sections.summary: Briquettes down 42.5 per cent for lack of pitch; Samchuk cement plant made 3,251 tons; pottery down 48.2 per cent; rubber shoes 43,578 pairs.

sections.title: Monopoly Bureau Products
sections.summary: Government salterns idle for a third month; cigarette output down 23.4 per cent; supplemental fund of 309,193,000 won for tobacco purchases.

sections.title: Section 6. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: Executive Order No. 12 created the consumer goods allocation machinery; allocations of civilian supply, petroleum and ex-Japanese materials; year-end bonus in kind of about 445 won for 500,000 employees.

sections.title: Reorganization of Allocation Procedures
sections.summary: Full text of Executive Order No. 12 (12 January) and its memorandum on priorities, eligibility, allocation and distribution through the Federation of Financial Associations.

sections.title: Allocations of Civilian Supply
sections.summary: Allocations to departments included 45,000 bags of cement and tractors to Agriculture, 1,500 rolls of asphalt roofing for housing, and zinc powder for Health.

sections.title: Petroleum
sections.summary: Petroleum Distributing Agency allocations included a 25 per cent gasoline increase voted by provincial officers and 1,000 extra drums of kerosene.

sections.title: Allocations of Ex-Japanese Materials
sections.summary: Surrendered Japanese goods allocated: brass and copper for souvenir makers, 400 submarine batteries, 100 tons of scrap, and 20 tons of zinc found at Inchon.

sections.title: Allocations of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: Maj. Gen. Dean approved a year-end bonus in kind for about 500,000 employees, valued near 445 won each, not yet distributed; tables of cloth, shoe, tire and soap allocations.

sections.title: Distribution of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: Federation of Financial Associations bought 30,246,000 won of goods and the Federation of Distributing Associations 65,784,000 won from vested factories; provincial distribution compared with population.

sections.title: Section 7. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade grew in 1947 (imports 2,088,125,206 won); December exports exceeded imports; Hong Kong trade; FLC surplus purchases; 57,889 tons of civilian supply arrived in January.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Gives a short 1947 trade summary alongside January 1948 activities. January statistics cover government-to-government and Civilian Supply imports; private trade figures follow next month.

sections.title: Private Trade Statistics
sections.summary: Barter trade rose after the Foreign Exchange Bank opened 15 July 1947; December imports 246,703,305 won, exports 271,691,240 won; 68 import and 103 export permits in January.

sections.title: Private Trade Activities
sections.summary: Hong Kong trade reopened August 1947 with two to three ships monthly; SS Sinkiang and Leopold Skeik cargoes; Pusan-Hong Kong freight HK$65 per ton.

sections.title: Government-to-Government Transactions
sections.summary: Hong Kong office closed December 1947; 1,350 tons of scheelite shipped to New York in 1947; exports to Japan valued at $2,510,736.30; apple shipments spoiled.

sections.title: Activities
sections.summary: Souvenir items worth $32,541.90 sold to Army Exchange Service; new Pusan office opened for export customers; mineral export stockpiles noted.

sections.title: Status of FLC Imports
sections.summary: Seven purchase agreements against a $25,000,000 FLC credit for surplus stocks from Japan, Philippines, Iwo Jima and Hawaii at 21 to 50 cents on the dollar.

sections.title: Other Civilian Supply Imports
sections.summary: 1947 imports from Japan $21,127,949 and from the US $69,830,725; 57,889 tons arrived in January, including 16,127 tons of sugar, fertilizer, coal and penicillin.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Yong Dong Po strike (8-16 January) and Seoul streetcar walkout; Tai Han No Chung Federation convention of 864 delegates; working-hours exemptions; child labor survey.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities, public works and housing: over 62 per cent of locomotives inoperative, a 60-fold electric rate rise, highway plans and 560 refugee houses.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: December revenue rose 113,000,000 won on a 115,000,000-won Army payment; over 62 per cent of locomotives inoperative; freight 138,000 tons below November; coal consumption down 20 per cent.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Railroads carry most freight and passengers; trucks and ox carts serve only short hauls. Lack of bituminous coal eliminated 107 of 262 scheduled trains through December, congesting ports.

sections.title: Income and Expenditures
sections.summary: Department revenue rose 113,000,000 won in December; expenditures rose as back bills were paid, including 81,000,000 won for Japanese coal.

sections.title: Railroads
sections.summary: Railroad income was 36 per cent above November owing to the Army payment; passenger, freight, equipment and employment tables follow.

sections.title: Marine Transportation
sections.summary: Marine revenue up 72 per cent and expenditures up 84 per cent owing to a 27,000,000-won back payment to seamen; passenger traffic lowest since February 1947.

sections.title: Air and Highway Transportation
sections.summary: Air Bureau expenditures rose sharply to repair control equipment at airports other than Kimpo; highway expenditures also increased.

sections.title: Supply Division
sections.summary: Daily coal reporting system set up; specifications completed for the Dan Yang sub-station to enable electric locomotives.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: December revenue rose 62 per cent to the highest since January 1946; 37,183 telephone users on 624 exchanges; 623 post offices; 175,000 radios and 11 stations.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The Interim Government's Department of Communications runs telephone, telegraph, radio and postal services; only the Korean Broadcasting Corporation is outside it. Postwar disrepair is being fixed with American and Japanese materials.

sections.title: Revenues and Expenditures
sections.summary: December revenue rose 25,700,000 won (62 per cent) after rate increases; expenditures still ran 30 per cent above revenue.

sections.title: Employment
sections.summary: Employment rose slightly for a second month as clerical staff shifted from postal to telephone, telegraph and radio sections.

sections.title: Special Functions
sections.summary: Post offices collect income, restaurant and tobacco taxes for the Department of Finance; tables of revenue, expenditures, employees and tax receipts.

sections.title: Postal Deposits and Insurance
sections.summary: Postal deposits fell while depositors rose; book transfer balances up 9,000,000 won; National Life Insurance policies grew steadily.

sections.title: Telephone and Telegraph
sections.summary: 2,000 people await telephones in Seoul; 624 exchanges serve 37,183 users; telegraph messages and revenue (up 32 per cent) rose in December.

sections.title: Postal Bureau
sections.summary: Classification of 623 post offices; two railway post offices at Seoul and Pusan and 23 mail cars.

sections.title: Radio
sections.summary: Korean Broadcasting Corporation monopoly: 11 stations, about 175,000 receivers (50,000 broken), 112,000 paying the 40-won monthly fee.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: 74,000,000 kwh delivered in January; Emergency Power Committee restricted use; streetcars fell from 137 to 30 during a walkout; Board recommended a 60-fold retail rate increase on 8 January.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Highway program continued despite a 367,000,000-won F/Y 1948/49 cut; Seoul-Kangnung survey funded at 300,000 won; 214 fires caused 135,218,400 won damage; Heavy Equipment school opened 12 January.

sections.title: Section 5. Housing
sections.summary: National Housing Administration stockpiled materials for low-cost Seoul houses; 560 refugee units completed in provinces and nearly all of 400 Seoul refugee houses finished.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance: note issue fell 1,767,000,000 won, supplementary appropriations, revenue 71 per cent of expenditure, bank deposits up 6,034 million won in December.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Notes outstanding fell 1,767,000,000 won; six supplementary appropriations over 601,000,000 won; revenue was 71 per cent of expenditure; Civilian Supply accounts receivable over 500,000,000 won.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-government Finance
sections.summary: December deposits rose 6,034 million won (15 per cent) and loans 4,801 million won; 'Fight Inflation With Life Insurance' campaign; Chosun Life capital increase; dishonored bills table.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, the Legislative Assembly, political reactions to the UN Commission, legal affairs, police and inter-zone activities, including the 9 January Kim Koo-Rhee merger.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: 400 tons of paper stockpiled for the UN election; Maritime Board preliminary report 15 January; National Economic Board approved rate increases and refused 100,000 pounds of Chinese sugar.

sections.title: Section 2. Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: Twelve sessions, average attendance 63 and frequent lack of quorum; debates on weights and measures, electric rates and prostitution; Philippine delegate Arranz visited 30 January.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Little action owing to missing quorum after the holiday recess; 12 sessions averaging 2 hours 45 minutes, 90 members authorized.

sections.title: Law for Weights and Measures
sections.summary: First reading of a law letting Commerce restrict the Chok-kwan system to enforce metric units; Won Se-hun objected; title approved 32 to 6.

sections.title: Electric Power
sections.summary: Assembly challenged the sixfold power rate announcement, summoned officials on 22 January and referred investigation to two committees.

sections.title: Public Prostitution Law
sections.summary: Debate on amending Public Act No. 7; a three-month delay of the effective date was rejected 37 to 7.

sections.title: Public Act No. 8
sections.summary: Revised Ordinance 153 passed as an act prohibiting aid to US personnel in violating military directives, with 'off limits' and prostitution provisions; penalty one year or 50,000 won.

sections.title: Other Business
sections.summary: First reading of Temporary Nationality Law provisions; 38 of 56 senior appointees approved; Assembly refused 30 to 0 to join a rice-collection commendation committee.

sections.title: Visit of Philippine Representative to UN Commission on Korea
sections.summary: Melecio Arranz addressed the 199th session on 30 January, conveying Philippine greetings; Dr. Kimm Kiu-sic thanked him.

sections.title: Section 3. Political Developments
sections.summary: Kim Koo and Rhee Syngman merged rightist groups on 9 January; Kimm Kiu-sic urged referral to the Little Assembly; Kim Koo proposed troop withdrawal and a leaders' conference.

sections.title: Section 4. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinances 161-166, Public Act No. 8 and Executive Order No. 12; opinions on KILA quorum and missionary customs duties; prison population statistics at 31 October 1947.

sections.title: Ordinances and Orders
sections.summary: Ordinances 161-166 covered automobile fees, vested property title and revising the Korea Agricultural Association; also Civil Service Rules No. 10.

sections.title: Legal Opinions
sections.summary: Justice opinions on enforcing KILA attendance, a vested company's funeral-expense liability (up to 1,000,000 won), the Theatrical Performance Law as censorship, and missionary car customs duties.

sections.title: Penal Institutions
sections.summary: 199 student guards enrolled 7 January; inspections of Inchon, Kaesong, Uijongbu and Ascom City camps; prison population tables of 31 October 1947.

sections.title: Korean Courts
sections.summary: UN legal counselor Dr. Marc Schreiber addressed judges and lawyers on 31 January; investigation of a Korean National Youth member's arrest at Wonju.

sections.title: Property Claims Commission
sections.summary: Final decisions were made in six property claims cases during January.

sections.title: Juvenile Courts
sections.summary: Juvenile court centers expanded to four provinces in 1947; lack of funds blocked wider extension.

sections.title: Section 5. Police
sections.summary: Korean National Police Women's Division trained policewomen at the Police Academy; a weekly report listed about 60 arrests including a wild-boar incident.

sections.title: Section 6. Inter-zone Activities
sections.summary: North-South mail exchanged once (10 January); Radio Pyongyang propaganda against the UN Commission, a North Korean constitution broadcast; Station HLKA counter-programming.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture, public information, press opinion, Korean National Youth (475,000 members) and the first Women's Activities section.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Mainly diphtheria, typhus and typhoid; Chongju health center opened 20 January; eight narcotics raids; 2,958 narcotics licenses; Sajik Park receiving home for 200 children.

sections.title: Vital Statistics
sections.summary: Monthly and annual tabulations of births, deaths, marriages and divorces planned; April-December 1946 mortality showed high infant deaths from pneumonia and similar diseases.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: Diphtheria, typhus and typhoid were the main communicable diseases; examination of licensed Seoul prostitutes before release planned.

sections.title: Medical Services
sections.summary: Chongju health center opened 20 January; tuberculosis training at Masan; Materia Medica translation; conditions at Chonju and Pusan hospitals and the Pusan leprosarium.

sections.title: Nursing Affairs
sections.summary: Nurse and midwife examination set for May 1948; Presbyterian Hospital School of Nursing accredited 26 January.

sections.title: Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: Meat inspection withdrawn from East Gate and Yong Dong Po slaughterhouses on 23 January; fish market building near Seoul Station returned to use.

sections.title: Pharmaceutical Affairs
sections.summary: Pharmacists examination planned for 25 March to 1 April; gauze capacity idle for lack of cotton; 400 tons of coal allocated to medical supply plants.

sections.title: Narcotics Section
sections.summary: Eight raids, 12 arrests; 52 investigators; raw opium rose from 1,200 to 3,000 won per 37 grams; 2,958 licenses issued, 2,752 to doctors.

sections.title: Laboratories
sections.summary: Biologicals production negligible for lack of power; fire destroyed an incubator at Anyang on 10 January.

sections.title: Public Assistance
sections.summary: 1,200 tons of powdered skim milk arrived at Pusan; Blind and Deaf School moved to Education; Sajik Park children's home opened 10 January.

sections.title: Women's Bureau
sections.summary: Conferences on abolishing legalized prostitution under Public Act No. 7 and housing displaced girls; travelers' aid started at Seoul Station 26 January.

sections.title: Welfare Supply
sections.summary: 4,000 mattresses sent to Pusan and 1,500 to the National Leprosarium at Sorokto.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: 13,579,080 won approved for a Teachers' Training Center opening about 1 July; 200,000,000-won elementary subsidy; textbooks; 111 students sent to the US; American Language Institute.

sections.title: Section 3. Culture
sections.summary: Lee Orchestra played for the UN Commission on 14 January; La Traviata sung in Korean from 16 January; Spring Fragrance drama; Korean American Cultural Association; athletics.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Information
sections.summary: 101 press releases and 23 foreign items issued; rice collection 93 per cent by 5 January; 31 January directive on press freedom; 16 political parties registered.

sections.title: Section 5. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press centered on the UN Commission, with rightist, leftist and moderate demands; rate-increase complaints; police plots and the attack on Chang Paik-sang; polls showing 53 per cent faced contribution demands.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: January 1948 Korean press focused on the UN Temporary Commission and the coming election; parties' demands dragged on, Commission arrived 8 January, and Kim Koo's late-month change of heart was the one surprise.

sections.title: New Year's Statements
sections.summary: Rightist Dae Han Ilbo warned the US to back Rhee and Kim Koo; leftists demanded troop withdrawal; both sides demanded release of political prisoners; moderates urged self-help.

sections.title: "World Situation in the New Year"
sections.summary: Cha Yoo Shin Mun surveyed global conflicts; leftist Chosun Ilbo on 20 January distrusted American friendliness toward Japan.

sections.title: UN Commission Activities
sections.summary: Papers fully covered the Commission; Dr. K. P. S. Menon elected temporary chairman; Soviet refusal to cooperate; Kim Koo's 28 January statement on free elections.

sections.title: "Racial Spirit"
sections.summary: Cha Yoo Shin Mun (4 January) urged a new national culture; Choong Ang Shin Mun (7 January) proposed cutting wedding and funeral costs, and attacked mammonism (18 January) and profit-driven publishing (29 January).

sections.title: Economic Discussions
sections.summary: Leftist Chosun Choong Ang Ilbo (5 January) blamed falling living standards on material shortages, bank-note over-issue and 20 percent plant output; Chosun Ilbo (18 January) said the land reform bill was stalled for lack of a quorum.

sections.title: Police
sections.summary: Police warned against disturbances and described alleged leftist plots, an attack on Metropolitan Chief Chang Paik-sang, the Chang Duk-soo murder case, and charges of police abuse.

sections.title: Public Opinion
sections.summary: Polls: 87.1 per cent expected North Korean currency changes to affect the South; 84 per cent opposed the electric rate rise; 88 per cent backed textbook-first publishing; 53 per cent faced contribution demands.

sections.title: Section 6. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Membership rose 15 per cent to 475,000, including 17,500 women and 10,000 students; training goal of 200,000; 550,000 daily service hours; threats from rivals such as Dai Dong.

sections.title: Section 7. Women's Activities
sections.summary: Women's Bureau cocktail party for the UN Commission 14 January; monthly meeting of eight provinces; new Federation of Women's Organizations; Mother's School opened; YWCA delegates feted.
